recoveredSpeechGaps.transcript: There was a girl called D. Wren who was eight and had nobody at all, and I walked her to her mother's cousin's people over two months. That is the single thing I have done in my life that I would do again in the same order. Ander Croft was 11 years old. He died about 40 feet from the bottom of the shed steps, and nobody ever wrote down what he had been able to do. Vera held a doorway. He set it into the fire. The long...

You take someone who has been called stubborn by his mother his entire life, and you tell him what he actually is. That is what Homura was for. Not the paper. The paper was only how they meant to say it. So I stood in a river, and I decided that I was going to do both, and that if I only got one of them, it had better be this one. Then I came up the bank and started answering Milo's questions. I never told any of you I'd decided anything.

transcript: Chapter 17. Homura. The fire they built was the biggest Torrin had sat at since Sallow Creek. It took the broken crate and the dry rafter ends out of the byre and a whole armful of old thorn off the wall, and when it caught properly, it went up eight feet and threw light on the inside of the yard walls all the way round. The slate on the gable went orange. The socket stones at the gap put shadows twelve feet long across the grass. Everybody's face was visible. That was the point of it. Torrin could see the shine on Milo's eyes, the line of Dessa's jaw, Senna's hands folded on the blanket, wick on his crate with the bar across his knees. Every one of them was lit like a thing in a shop window, and out past the wall the dark had got much darker, the way it does. Rook sat down on the flat stone with the fire between him and all of them, and pushed his left sleeve back, and undid the buckle. He took the strap off and put it down on the stone beside him with the small dark oval lying in its stitched hide pocket, face up, where the light got at it. Nobody said anything. The skin underneath was two shades paler than the rest of the forearm. It had a permanent groove worn into it by years of the same buckle at the same tension, and a white line across the outside edge where something had once gone through leather and skin together. I'll come back to that, Rook said. He put his hands on his knees, palms open. Right. I'm going to do this in order, and I'd ask you to let me. If I go out of order, I'll stop, and I do not think I would start again. He looked at the fire rather than at any of them. It starts a long way from here, and it takes a while to get to anything you'd recognize. Don't help me along. There's a village called Lowry Bend, he said. It's about 400 miles southeast of the rock cut, which means none of you have ever heard of it, and nor has anybody else. 90 people. A river with a kink in it, which is where the name comes from, and a bridge with a hole in it that had been there since before the fall. It's a hand village. He turned his own palm over. That's what they called it. The trade there was hands. There were nine women and two men in that village who could do what Marta Faust did at a rock cut, and they did it for a living. Most of it wasn't walls. Most of it was a broken arm set properly at four in the morning, and a fever held down for two days, and a calf turned in a cow. He said it flatly, as information. Nobody in Lowry Bend had ever seen an ember. I want you to understand that. Not a rumor of one, and not a bad one. Nobody in that village had held the thing in their hand, ever, in four generations. It was a story about people in the north. My mother was the best of the eleven. She had a way of putting her hands on the outside of a thing, and finding the inside of it that I never saw anybody else manage in my life. She taught it to fourteen people. It was the whole of her. I've got two brothers. Had. Both younger. One of them followed her into it and was going to be better than her, and one of them could not have mended a shoe. Milo laughed and stopped himself instantly. No, Rook said. You're right. That's what he was like. That's exactly what he was like. I was kindled at thirteen, he said, and nothing happened. Dessa did not move. Nothing happened for eleven months. My mother put her hands on me every week for the first three and then stopped, because she could feel there was nothing to put them on, and she was not going to lie to me about it. There was no word for me in that village. The nearest they had was late, which is a kind word, and does a lot of damage. Eleven months, said Dessa. Eleven months. I had thirteen, and two. I know, Rook said. I have known it since a way yard at Hob's Wall. It is the entire reason I went down to that beck, and I'd have told you so eleven days ago if I could have done it without telling you the rest. Dessa Cole sat with her bad leg out straight in front of her and did not say one word. Then it came, said Milo. Then it came. In the eleventh month, in the dark, on the bridge with the hole in it, which is a whole other evening and not the one we're having. He shifted. What matters about it is that it came through my mother's door, because that was the only door anybody in that place had ever heard of. I was a hand. Fourteen years old and a hand. And about a fifth as good at it as she was at twenty, and extremely pleased with myself. There was a man who came through with a cart when I was fourteen, Rook said. He came twice a year with medicine and a doctor, and he had done it for six years before he ever spoke to me. That's how it works. You don't arrive somewhere and offer to buy a child. You arrive for six years with a doctor, and then you're the man with the doctor. Senna made a small noise in the cart. Rook did not stop. He was looking for children who'd come up through a single tradition in a place that had only got the one. That was the whole requirement. Not talent, purity if you like. Which is a foul word for it and the right one. He wanted people who had never once in their lives heard a second explanation of anything. What he paid was not money. They never paid in money. They paid in kind, and what he put on my mother's table was a doctor twice a year for the whole village, and a standing debt they could draw medicine against, and her own course of treatment for a thing in her chest that had started the winter before. He stopped for a second. I was bought, he said. That is the plain word. I have never found a better one, and I have had eleven years to look. And I would have gone anyway. She knew I would have gone anyway. Neither of us ever said so. Did she live? said Milo. For nine more years. She never used most of it. She kept giving her turns at the doctor away to other people's children, which is a thing I did not find out until it was much too late to have an argument with her about it. The place they took me to was called Homura, Rook said. The word went out into the yard and the fire took it. Torrin realized about a half second afterward that he had been waiting twenty-eight days for a word and had no idea what to do with it now that he had one. It did not sound like anything. It sounded like a place. Say it back, Rook said. Homura, said Milo. That's it. Two hundred miles north of Lowry Bend, in a valley about a mile and a half long with a cliff at the top end. And it was built on purpose, on a fracture. He picked up a bit of thorn and turned it over. You've all seen ground that's turning. Cass Ordway's ground. And the drove road and the bad country south of the wall that a factor had been told about for five weeks. A fracture is that permanent. It is a place where the tearing does not stop. There was a wormhole opening in the top of that valley roughly every nine days for the whole of the time I lived there. And about a third of them put something through. You lived there, said Wyke. Sixty of us. Forty were children. Rook put the thorn on the fire. You do not study a thing by going and standing where it isn't. The man who ran it was called Oren Vel. He was five foot nothing and about fifty, with a voice like a nail going into a plank. Every single person in that valley was frightened of him, including the grown researchers, including the two men whose job it was to stand in the top of the valley with a spear. Rook's mouth did something that was not quite anything. I have met a great many frightening men since. He is still the only one who ever frightened me by being correct at me. He built it with forty children from nine different traditions, on purpose. He told us why on the first morning I was there, and every morning after, nine traditions. Hand villages like mine. Stone clans from the north where the ember goes down eight generations. Two boys off a cultivation road who had never touched either, and could stand in a river in December. A girl from somewhere southeast whose people did the whole thing by singing, which I still do not entirely believe, and which measured the same as everybody else's. And he paired us. Every test. Every day, for four years, you and somebody from another tradition doing the same thing at the same time with the same instruments on both of you. Rook looked up. Say why. Nobody said anything. Dessa, he said. You know this one. Dessa's chin came up. Because on your own, you'd explain it with your own words, she said slowly. And your own words would fit. They'd always fit. So you'd never find out they were the wrong ones. Yes. Rook nodded once. You cannot get outside your own tradition by thinking hard. You can only get outside it by being tied at the wrist to somebody whose tradition is different and who is as sure as you are. What was it like? Said Milo. Milo. Dessa started. No, that's a fair question, and I'd rather have it now. Rook thought about it for a second, which he almost never did. It was cold. It was always cold, because of the cliff. The food was bad in a very organized way. There was a noise the fracture made when it was about to go, and you learned it in a fortnight. To this day I cannot hear a kettle coming to the boil without my shoulders going up. And it was the best place I have ever been in my life. He said that flatly too, which somehow made it worse. Forty children who had all been the strange one in their own village in one valley, with somebody asking them questions and writing down the answers. Nobody was late there. Nobody was the cripple, or the freak, or the one whose door didn't open. There was a boy there with no hands who ran the third instrument bench, and I never once heard anybody remark on it. We traded. That's the part I think about. Nine traditions of children in one valley, and inside a year we were all quietly teaching each other things we'd been told at home were impossible, and getting in trouble for it, and doing it anyway behind the drying shed. There was a girl called Vera Kess, he said. The fire cracked. Nobody moved at all. She was a year older than me. Stone clan. Eight generations of it. Up on the north side of the marches. One of the old ones that had kept more of its own vocabulary than most clans bother to. That matters. Remember that she had words nobody else had. And I hated her for about a year, Senna said. Ah. Hand against stone. It's the oldest argument in the world, and it has been going for a hundred and fifty years. The two of us refought the whole of it in miniature in a cold valley, at fourteen and fifteen, at the top of our voices. Rook's hands had not moved off his knees. She thought a hand was a trick. She thought it was something a person did with their face and their manner, and that it worked because people wanted it to, and that a hand village was ninety people agreeing to be fooled. She had a great deal of evidence. I thought the stone was a crutch. I thought anybody who needed a lump of metal strapped to their arm to reach the inside of themselves had been sold something, and that her whole clan were eight generations of people who had never once tried it without. We were both completely wrong, and we were wrong in exactly the same way. It took me six years to see that. She saw it at fifteen. The valley got opened in my second year, Rook said. That's what we called it. The fracture put something through at the top end that the two men with the spears could not hold, and it came down the valley in the middle of the afternoon and went into the long shed where the younger ones were. Vera was in that shed. He stopped. It was the first time he had stopped since he started, and Torrin, on the other side of a fire, watched a man take a breath the way a person takes a step onto a floor they are not sure of. She got eleven of them out and went back for two more and held the door. She held it. They got out. And the thing went through her while she was doing it. And there was nobody young enough to help her. That's the part nobody understands when I tell it. So I'll say it properly. The station had grown healers. Three of them. And they were good. And they were at the top of the valley doing the other half of the disaster, and they did not get down to the shed for two hours. He looked at his own open hands. Two hours. And there were fourteen hand-tradition children in that valley, of which I was the second oldest. And every one of us had been taught the same thing at home, which is that you do not put your hands on a bad wound before a grown one does, because you can set it wrong and lock it there. So I stood outside a door for nine hours and did nothing. I was fifteen. That's the number I'd like you all to have. Fifteen. With my mother's hands on the end of my arms, standing in a corridor. She lived, Rook said. I want that said quickly, because I can see four faces and one of them's gone white. She lived. She was up in six weeks. She was never quite right in the left shoulder after it, and she used to say that was a bargain. But I sat outside that door for nine hours, and somewhere in the middle of the night I stopped being able to find the argument. I went looking for it. It was mine. I had had it for a year, and it was a large part of what I was made of at fifteen. It was simply not in the room anymore. I couldn't locate it. It had gone the way a tune goes. And then, said Torrin, he had not meant to speak. And then they let me in in the morning, and she was gray and furious and could not sit up, Rook said. And I said something to her that I am not going to repeat at this fire. And she looked at me for a while. And then she said, You've got it wrong. I've got it wrong. It's the same wrongness both ways. I've known for a year, and there is nobody in this valley I can tell. She had a word for it, Rook said. Her clan had kept it. Most of them had dropped it about four generations back, because it did not mean anything useful anymore, and you cannot sell it at a gate. Hers hadn't. The word is Satori. He said it into the fire. Torrin did not know what to do with his hands. Say it, Rook said. Satori, said Dessa. Satori, said Milo. Wick said it too. Torrin heard his own voice go with theirs about a half beat late, and afterward he could never work out whether it had been a strange thing to do or the only available thing. Right, Rook said. I have thought about how to say this part for eleven years, and have never once had to do it out loud, so it will come out poorly, and you're going to have it poorly. Everything you have ever been told about where power comes from is a description of a door. The stone tradition says it lives in the metal. That's not a stupid thing to believe. You strap the metal on, and the thing happens. You take the metal off, and it doesn't. Any sensible person concludes the metal is where it lives. My hand village said it comes from outside that the tearing put something loose into the world, and that a person with a knack is a person who can catch hold of what's going past. Also not stupid. Also fits everything you can see. And the cultivation road says it's in the body, and you build it over twenty years like a wall. All three of them are right about what they can see, and all three of them are wrong about the same thing in the same place. He put one hand flat in the air and turned it over. It is one force. There is one thing, and it comes from inside a person. The stone, the hand, and the twenty years are three different handles on the same door. Every tradition has mistaken its own handle for the whole house. Vera worked that out on her own at fifteen, in a valley full of instruments, and told nobody for a year because there was nobody in that valley who was not the child of one of the three answers. And Satori is the moment the door goes, he said. That's all it is. Not a power. Not a rank and not a trick. And there is nothing at the end of it to pick up and take away. It is the second in which a person stops believing their own handle is the house. And what's on the other side turns out to be the same light that was on the other side of all of them. It has two halves. I have given both of them to two of you already, and neither of you knew what I was quoting. An empty mind. Meaning you put down every single thing you have ever been told about where the power lives and what it looks like and who's allowed to have it. Including mine. And an open soul. Meaning you stop guarding because a thing that is inside you can be guarded against. And most people have spent their whole lives getting extremely good at not letting anything out from in there where it might get looked at. He turned his head. Connected, he said. Those two things at once. That's the whole teaching. Her clan called it the path. I have never found a better name for it. And I have stopped trying. Dessa had both her hands flat on the ground. That's what you said to me at the beck, she said. Word for word. It's hers. It's hers. I have never in my life used a word of it that wasn't hers. And I did it. You did it, Rook said. Four seconds, said Dessa. Her voice had gone somewhere. Torrin had never heard it go. Four seconds. And I've tried it every night since and got nothing at all. You told me that was the shape of it. And I thought you were being kind. I have never been kind to you once. And I'm not going to start tonight. Rook did not soften it at all. It is the shape of it. Vera did it at fifteen and could not do it again for four months. And in eleven years on the other side of everything that happened afterward, I have seen it twice. One of them is sitting on my left with her leg out straight. Eight. The other one was a boy called Andercroft. He was eleven. He did it in front of six people at the second instrument bench and Oren Vel had to sit down on the floor. Rook stopped. You'll want to know what happened to him and I'm coming to it, he said. Don't ask yet. They measured it, he said. That's the whole of what Homura was. It is the part nobody ever cares about. And it is the only part that would have mattered. Vel believed her. That's the thing about him. A sixteen-year-old girl with a bad shoulder told a man who had been right about everything for thirty years that the foundation of all nine traditions was a misunderstanding. And he listened to her for two hours and then went and changed the entire program. After that it was one question. Do nine traditions measure the same or don't they? Four years. Every ninth day matched readings, cross-paired. Every child in that valley and every adult who would sit still for it. Instruments on both. And by hand as well. Well, because the instruments were pre-fall and cranky and Vel trusted a trained person's own report as much as he trusted a needle. He looked up. They called that a redding, he said. A proper one. With the fractions set out loud about a fifth of the rooms lit. About half. About a quarter and falling. It's a Homura word. I have not heard anybody outside that valley use it. And I have not said it in front of another person in eleven years. You'll hear it from me from now on. Because it is a better tool than anything else I've got. And there is no longer any reason not to. And did they? Said Wyke. Measure the same. Yes. The fire popped. Identical. Rook said. Not similar. Not close enough to argue about. Nine traditions. Four years. Matched instruments and matched hands. And the shape of the thing that happened inside a person was the same shape every time. And it had nothing whatever to do with which door they came through. Two more years and it would have been written up and copied out and sent to every station and every hall and every teaching house that would take one. It was going to end the oldest argument in the world with a column of numbers. And on the eleventh of the ninth month, Rook said, cinder company came over the wire. Nobody breathed. I was nineteen. It was about two in the morning and the fracture was quiet. Which matters. Because the first thing all forty of us thought was that it had gone off. They came over the west wire in the dark. Quietly. In order. It was not a rush. Nothing about it was a rush. His voice had not changed at all and Torrin wanted. Suddenly and violently. For it too. They had been on that valley for days. They knew where the papers were. They knew where the instrument benches were. They knew which of the sixty of us could do anything about it. And they went to those people first. And the first thing they did before anything. Before one hand was laid on one person was take the gate. Torrin's whole body went cold from the top down. He was not on a hillside. He was lying on wet turf beside a hundred and sixty year old brick kiln at some hour after midnight. Going through a piece of ground the way he had been taught to go through a piece of ground. Three men stood across the gate and did not move. Everybody else was moving. Why would you put three men on an open gate you had already come through? You don't put people across a gate to keep anybody out. Torrin said. His voice came out wrong. No, said Rook. There's nothing left outside to keep out. You put them there so nobody in the yard can use it. Yes. At Cold Harbor. Torrin could hear himself and could not stop. At the wharf. On the mud. With the boots that went from mud to puddle. You told us everything. You told us about the gate off its hinges and the tidy pile and the four nail holes and the clean rectangle on the shelf. And you didn't tell us that? That's what a shape like that costs and everybody at this fire has watched somebody pay it. Milo had his hands over his mouth. I got to her, Rook said. That is the one piece of luck in the whole of that night and I have never once been able to decide what it was worth. I had about four minutes. I do not know who took it. I do not know who paid a company of nine people to come a very long way and lift four years of paper off a cold valley in the middle of the night. In eleven years I have not found one honest answer to that. And I have stopped expecting to. So I made her a promise and I did not keep it. That's the account. Everything else is arrangement. And looked at it the way a man looks at a tool he has used for years. This is hers, he said. Torrin heard Senna Vos draw a breath in the cart. I took it off the floor of the room she died in. It was nine feet from her and the strap had come off it. I picked it up because I was nineteen and I could not leave it lying on a floor. I have worn it every day since. Eleven years. He put it back down on the stone. I have not said that out loud to another living person. Not to anybody who got over the wire. Not to D-Ren's people. Not to a single one of the seven or eight I'd have called a friend since. Eleven years. So there it is. That's the whole of Homura and I'd like a minute before the rest of it. Milo was crying without making any noise about it, which he had got very good at. Dessa had not moved at all. And he was looking at the small dark oval lying on a stone in the firelight, twelve feet away, with nobody's arm around it. Rook came back and sat down. Dessa, he said. You took it off your own arm and you strapped it onto mine. Two holes in from where you wear it. Yes. Because it was cut for a girl. Because it was cut for a girl, Rook said. And because I have had that thing on my arm for eleven years, and it has never once done for me what it did for her. I have always assumed that was because of me. I want that stated at this fire because it is true and because I have had eleven years to want it to be otherwise. They were two entirely separate holes in me. I went round both of them every day. It never once occurred to me that they might be the same hole. Because nobody says a company's name in a village square. They say the company, they say those fellows. And I had been in a valley with my hands over my head in the dark. And at nineteen I never heard anybody say a name at all. It was a bootmaker, Rook said. Six years ago in a market town I will not name. On a Thursday. He had a tray of salvage on the counter. Buckles, buttons, cord ends. The sort of tray a man keeps for people who need one of something. And there were four bits of brass in it with holes punched in the edge. He was selling them as button blanks. He turned one over in front of me to show me the flat side. And there was a number on it and a mark under the number. Rook put his hand inside his coat and took the chit out. He held it up between two fingers, small and square with the corners taken off. And the firelight found it. Torrin, nine feet away, could see the chevron with the line struck through it, cut poorly off center by somebody in a hurry a long time ago. I had been looking at that mark for four days on a cliff road while nine competent men worked above my village, Rook said.
